description: We are a group of ambitious students that are interested in applying theoretical classroom-like principles into the real world and making an impact with them.
summary: NASA is planning Moon habitats with oxygen-rich air, yet much of the fire-test evidence behind spacecraft materials was gathered under different conditions. REDLINE, built by The Embers for Flame in Freefall, makes that gap visible. Load a lunar rover's bill of materials, click any part, and see which NASA Physical Sciences Informatics experiments tested that material, how their oxygen, pressure and gravity compare with your proposed scenario, and what was never tested. Every match, mismatch and gap links back to the original source. Our team checked all 45 evidence records against those sources, and one click exports a traceable review brief for the next research step. It runs in a browser, needs no API key, and keeps any AI explanation separate from the evidence. REDLINE does not predict fire safety or certify materials; it shows what the evidence supports and what it does not.
details:
REDLINE: see exactly what NASA's fire research does and does not tell us about a material

Team: The Embers | Challenge: Flame in Freefall

THE PROBLEM

Future Moon habitats and rovers will use materials in oxygen-rich, low-pressure, low-gravity air. Fire behavior depends on all of those conditions, but much of the available combustion evidence was gathered under other ones. A researcher asking "has anyone tested this material under conditions like ours?" must dig through scattered investigations, reports and datasets, then decide by hand how close each experiment really is. Gaps are easy to miss, and nothing is traceable for the next person.

WHAT WE BUILT

REDLINE is a browser-based research-review tool that turns that question into a clear, auditable answer. The central question is never "is this material safe?" It is "which NASA experiments are relevant to this proposed use, how close are their conditions, and what is still unsupported?"

HOW A RESEARCHER USES IT

1. Load the lunar rover demo, or import a bill of materials as CSV. Each rover part is linked to a material.

2. Click a part in the 3D rover view or the material list. REDLINE pulls up the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics experiments that tested that material.

3. Set a proposed scenario: oxygen concentration, pressure and gravity. REDLINE compares it condition by condition with what each experiment actually reported, and marks each one as matching, mismatched or missing. Missing values are never turned into a reassuring score.

4. Open the original source behind any row. All 45 current evidence records have been checked by our team against those sources.

5. Pin a baseline, change one condition at a time, and see the evidence picture shift.

6. Export a Markdown or JSON review brief with source identifiers, original conditions, notes, review status and an ordered list of follow-up research questions. The JSON can be reopened later, so a colleague can pick up exactly where the reviewer stopped.

WHY IT MATTERS AND WHO IT HELPS

Spacecraft material researchers, students and multidisciplinary teams get the material, the source, the experimental context and the unanswered question in one workflow. The benefit is a faster, clearer and auditable handoff: another person can see why a source was considered and what additional review or testing is needed. We have not measured time savings, adoption, predictive accuracy or reduced fire risk, and we do not claim them.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

REDLINE is built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigation metadata: a source-linked catalog of 26 entries (including umbrella and derived studies, not 26 independent datasets). Separate evidence records connect material-level questions to attributed experiments and reports. REDLINE interprets the relationship between a requested scenario and the documented evidence; it does not replace experimental support with a language model's confidence.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Most tools offer a single fire-risk number. REDLINE refuses to, and shows instead exactly which conditions match, conflict or are missing, then turns each gap into a concrete next research check. The spatial rover view makes the question tangible: click a real component, get its evidence trail. The rover and its material assignments are illustrative, not an authenticated NASA bill of materials.

We built REDLINE like a buffet: many tools, each doing the one job it is best at, all serving from the same table. Every task was a GitHub issue in one shared queue, and Claude and Codex agents on two computers each picked a task and worked on it separately. Every change had to pass the automated tests and the build, and one our team members reviewed it, before an autonomous merger added it to the app, so a broken change could never skip the line.

 

REDLINE itself works the same way. All 45 NASA evidence records sit on one shared table, and each part of the app does one job: NASA sources supply the evidence, filters find the records for your material, the comparison checks oxygen, pressure and gravity, and the 3D rover helps you find the part. You pick any part and REDLINE serves only the NASA tests for that material. A label is only shown when it is backed by a verified record, every record links to its NASA source, and AI helps organize the work but never replaces the NASA evidence or a person's sign-off.

 

REDLINE's numbers come straight from NASA, not from us. The cabin conditions of 34% oxygen at 56.5 kPa come from NASA's Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (2022), Section 4.6.3.6, and every evidence record comes from NASA test reports and NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository, such as the BASS-II and MIST experiments on the International Space Station. Each record keeps its NASA source, page and table, so anyone can check it in one click, which makes the evidence as reliable as the NASA research behind it. REDLINE does not claim certification or compliance with any NASA standard; it shows NASA's own results.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

JavaScript ES modules, HTML and CSS with static JSON/CSV data and a vendored Three.js viewer; React Aria Components and Lucide React for interface components; esbuild for the component bundle; Node.js's built-in test runner and jsdom for automated tests. Git and GitHub issues and pull requests coordinated the team; GitHub Pages hosts the public prototype. Claude and Codex assisted with code, research extraction, writing and review. The video's English narration is synthetic and its concept visuals are labeled.

AI AND PRIVACY

Evidence retrieval is deterministic keyword and field search, needs no API key and sends nothing anywhere. Optional AI explanations require a key the user supplies, are kept separate from the review brief, and are marked as generated. Having no AI for evidence retrieval eliminates the risk of hallucinations entirely. This makes our system optimal for researchers while the optional AI allows our system to align with the purposes of students too. Citations are not treated as proof that a generated statement is correct.

LIMITATIONS WE STATE OPENLY

Matching conditions does not establish safety. Partial-gravity evidence is limited, experimental methods differ between studies, and missing is not the same as zero. REDLINE is not a fire simulator, a material certification system, an operational emergency monitor or a NASA-endorsed product. Human review and further validation remain necessary.
